blocks.text: Upon entering he very nearly fell, for behind the door there was yet another step. “They do not show much consideration for the public,” he said. “They show no consideration at all,” said the court attendant, “just look here at the waiting room.” It was a long corridor, from which roughly carpentered doors led to the individual sections of the attic. Although there was no direct admission of light, it was nevertheless not completely dark, for some sections had, facing the corridor, instead of solid plank walls, mere wooden lattices—reaching, to be sure, right to the ceiling—through which a little light penetrated and through which one could also see individual officials as they wrote at tables or stood right up at the lattice and watched the people in the corridor through the gaps. There were, probably because it was Sunday, only a few people in the corridor. They made a very modest impression. At almost regular intervals from one another they sat upon the two rows of long wooden benches that were set along both sides of the corridor. All were negligently dressed, although most of them, by their facial expression, bearing, style of beard, and many scarcely ascertainable little details, belonged to the upper classes. Since no coat hooks were provided, they had placed their hats, probably each following the example of the next, under the bench. When those who sat nearest the door caught sight of K. and the court attendant, they rose in greeting; seeing this, those following thought themselves obliged to greet them as well, so that all rose as the two walked past. They never stood completely upright; their backs were bowed, their knees bent, they stood like street beggars. K. waited for the court attendant, who was walking a little behind him, and said, “How humiliated they must be.” “Yes,” said the court attendant, “they are defendants, all those you see here are defendants.” “Really!” said K. “Why, then they are my colleagues.” And he turned to the nearest one, a tall, slender, already almost gray-haired man. “What are you waiting for here?” asked K. politely. The unexpected address, however, threw the man into confusion, which looked all the more painful as he was evidently a man of the world who elsewhere certainly knew how to control himself and did not lightly surrender the superiority he had acquired over many. Here, however, he did not know how to answer so simple a question and looked toward the others as though they were obliged to help him, and as though no one could demand an answer of him if such help were not forthcoming. Then the court attendant stepped up and said, in order to calm and encourage the man, “The gentleman here is only asking what you’re waiting for. Go on, answer.” The voice of the court attendant, probably familiar to him, had a better effect: “I am waiting—” he began, and faltered. Evidently he had chosen this beginning so as to answer the precise wording of the question, but now could not find the continuation. Several of those waiting had drawn nearer and stood around the group; the court attendant said to them, “Away, away, clear the corridor.” They drew back a little, though not as far as their former seats. Meanwhile the man questioned had collected himself and even answered with a slight smile, “A month ago I made some applications for evidence in my case and am waiting for their disposition.” “You certainly seem to go to a great deal of trouble,” said K. “Yes,” said the man, “after all, it is my case.” “Not everyone thinks as you do,” said K.; “I, for example, am also accused, yet, as truly as I hope for salvation, I have neither filed an application for evidence nor undertaken anything else of the sort. Do you really consider that necessary?” “I do not know for certain,” said the man, once again in complete uncertainty; he evidently believed K. was having a jest with him, and therefore, for fear of committing some new error, he would probably best have liked to repeat his earlier answer in full, yet before K.’s impatient gaze he merely said, “as for myself, I have filed applications for evidence.” “You presumably do not believe that I am accused,” asked K. “Oh, please, certainly,” said the man, and stepped a little aside, yet in the answer there was not belief, but only fear. “So you do not believe me?” asked K., and took him by the arm, unconsciously invited to do so by the man’s humble demeanor, as though he wished to compel him to believe. He did not wish to cause him pain, and indeed had taken hold of him only very lightly, yet despite this the man cried out as though K. had gripped him not with two fingers, but with red-hot tongs. This ridiculous screaming wearied K. once and for all; if they did not believe that he was accused, so much the better; perhaps the man even took him for a judge. And now in parting he really did seize him more firmly, shoved him back onto the bench, and walked on. “Most defendants are so sensitive,” said the court attendant. Behind them almost all those waiting now gathered around the man, who had already ceased screaming, and seemed to be questioning him closely about the incident. Toward K. there now came a warder, recognizable chiefly by a saber whose scabbard, at least in color, consisted of aluminum. K. marveled at this and even reached out his hand toward it. The warder, who had come on account of the screaming, asked about what had happened. The court attendant sought to calm him with a few words, but the warder declared that he must nevertheless go and look for himself, saluted, and walked on with very hurried, yet very short steps, probably measured out by gout.
